name: Dihexa
evidenceNote: Every result comes from rats and cultured brain cells. The paper that proposed how dihexa works was retracted in 2025, and the main rat study carries a 2021 expression of concern. No study in people has been published, and the FDA says it has found no human exposure data.
summary: Dihexa is a lab-made fragment of angiotensin IV that improved maze learning in rats. It has never been tested in people and is not FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: Dihexa is a small modified peptide built from angiotensin IV, designed by Washington State University researchers to reach the brain when swallowed. In rats with chemically induced or age-related memory loss it improved water maze performance and increased the number of connections between neurons. That is the whole evidence base: no human trial exists, the 2014 paper that explained its mechanism was retracted in 2025, and the 2013 rat study carries an expression of concern. It is not FDA-approved, it is not eligible for routine compounding, and the FDA says it has no human safety data. Products sold online are unregulated research chemicals.

blocks.text: Dihexa is a synthetic, chemically modified peptide fragment. Its full chemical name is N-hexanoic-Tyr-Ile-(6) aminohexanoic amide, which describes a two-amino-acid core (tyrosine and isoleucine) capped at each end with fatty chains. It was built in the laboratory of Joseph Harding at Washington State University as a drug candidate for dementia [1].

The starting point was angiotensin IV, a short fragment of the blood pressure hormone angiotensin. Earlier work had shown that some angiotensin IV relatives improve memory in animals, but they break down quickly and cannot cross from the gut into the blood or from the blood into the brain. The team trimmed the active part down to three amino acids, then modified the ends to resist digestion and pass those barriers. Dihexa was the most stable and brain-penetrant version they produced [1].
Dihexa is sometimes marketed as a nootropic (a substance claimed to enhance thinking). That marketing runs well ahead of the science, which has never moved beyond animals.

items.text: The Harding group reports that dihexa, taken by mouth, reverses memory deficits in rats given scopolamine and in aged rats [1].
A follow-up paper proposes that dihexa works by binding hepatocyte growth factor and strengthening its signaling through the c-Met receptor [2].
The journal retracts the 2014 mechanism paper [3]. The same year, a phase 2/3 trial of fosgonimeton, a different HGF-targeting drug, misses its main goals in Alzheimer's disease [7].
The FDA says its compounding advisory committee will review dihexa acetate at a meeting to be held before the end of February 2027 [5].

blocks.text: The proposed mechanism centres on hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), a signaling protein best known for tissue repair, and its receptor, c-Met. In the brain, this pair helps neurons grow dendritic spines, the small projections where synapses (the junctions between nerve cells) form. The 2014 study reported that dihexa binds HGF tightly and makes small amounts of it far more effective at switching on c-Met [2].

In that work, dihexa increased spine and synapse formation in cultured rat hippocampal neurons, and the effect disappeared when HGF was blocked or c-Met was silenced. Blocking HGF inside the brain also cancelled dihexa's benefit on a maze task in rats [2].

That paper has since been retracted [3], so the mechanism should be treated as unconfirmed. The earlier 2013 study, which showed the memory effect without explaining it, has not been retracted [1]. In 2021, though, the journal placed an expression of concern on it, as it did on the 2014 paper, over possible image manipulation [8][9]. Online claims about dihexa's potency compared with natural growth factors come from cell experiments, not from measurements in a living brain.
No. Dihexa has never been approved by the FDA or any other major regulator, and no clinical trial of it appears on ClinicalTrials.gov, the federal registry where human drug studies are listed.

Dihexa acetate was nominated for use by compounding pharmacies, and the FDA placed it in Category 2 of its interim policy, the group it flags for safety concerns. In its assessment the agency said it had not identified any human exposure data for any route of administration and lacked important information on whether the substance would harm people. The nomination was later withdrawn, which leaves dihexa outside the substances compounders may routinely use [4].

The FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee is due to consider dihexa acetate at a meeting to be held before the end of February 2027 [5]. A committee vote is advice to the agency, not an approval. Dihexa was not among the six peptides covered by the October 2026 federal enforcement discretion policy.

The published research on dihexa itself is a small set of rodent and cell studies from one laboratory, and the journal has questioned the images in both key papers [8][9]. A 2026 review of peptides marketed for musculoskeletal and recovery uses grouped dihexa with other neuroactive peptides and noted the absence of clinical trials [6].

rows: Rats given scopolamine, and aged rats
Oral dihexa improved water maze learning and increased synapse formation; expression of concern since 2021 [8]
Effects depended on HGF and c-Met; paper retracted in 2025 [3]
No published or registered study in people

blocks.text: The closest human evidence concerns a different molecule. Fosgonimeton is a small drug designed to enhance the same HGF and c-Met system. In the LIFT-AD trial, 287 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease received fosgonimeton or placebo for 26 weeks. The drug did not meet its primary or secondary endpoints, though it was generally well tolerated [7]. That result does not test dihexa directly, but it is the largest trial so far of the idea dihexa is built on.
Safety in people is unknown. In its review, the FDA said it had found no human exposure data for dihexa by any route and could not tell whether the substance would cause harm if given to humans [4].

Dihexa is sold by research chemical websites as capsules, powders, and creams, usually labeled not for human consumption. These products are not made under drug manufacturing rules, and their identity, purity, and dose are not verified by any regulator. Anyone taking them is using a compound whose effects in humans have never been measured, and whose mechanism rests on a retracted paper [3].
